sas.summary: Winning in Big D and signing an athletic wing prospect (Flight White) so late gives SA plenty to offset what LeBron did to Duncan (and everyone else) Friday night.
November doesn't typically mean much to Spurs, but Oberto and Elson already have Duncan feeling good about the frontcourt help he's going to be getting.
You're tempted to question Spurs' age (and everything else) after a home L to Charlotte … except that only two of the six reigning division champs are over .500.
Losing yet another nail-biter with Dallas, Spurs can live with. Losing Ginobili on a hard fall, when he wasn't at his best to begin with, was much more disconcerting.
Not that they really need to look for silver linings, but Spurs are still unbeaten on the road with Manu in the lineup. So they're fine . . . as long as he's back soon.
Top spot was all theirs if Spurs had handled Lakers. The consolation: Manu is back and, easing into it after a back injury, has scored 45 points in his last 44 minutes.
Spurs aren't just rolling. They're cruising, with Duncan having topped 20 points just three times in December while averaging a mere 12.6 FGA per game this month.
Cruising? Spurs snoozed in a home loss to McGrady-less Houston and lost their only two games this month against teams with winning records as of Christmas morning.
If you were waiting for Pop's annual December rant about his team's lack of toughness, you got it at Christmas when he said Spurs have lost ''passion'' for D.
Swept by Cavs, shredded by Nowitzki, 0-2 at home against Dallas and now Parker has a bad hip? Maybe this little rankings tumble is the spark creaky Spurs need.
Don't waste your time. You can't convince me that Spurs' best week since November, including a total shutdown of Wiz, wasn't a direct response to their drop here to No. 7.
This week's comment comes from Pop, via our pal Peter May of the Boston Globe: ''It's hard for us to be as hungry as Phoenix or Dallas . . . and I understand that.''
Sympathy for Spurs is in short supply, even though they're a mere 8-6 in January. Reason being: Spurs are on a 57-25 pace and still have the NBA's third-best record.
In their last two title seasons? In '02-03, Spurs were also 32-16 after 48 games. Yet in '04-05, they were a tidy 38-10, six games ahead of Mavs instead of seven behind.
It's going to take wins in Jersey and Detroit -- on a back-to-back -- just for Spurs to finish .500 on the Rodeo Road Trip they always use as their annual springboard.
The next defeat will match last season's total. Yet you write them off at your own peril, after Spurs prevailed in Detroit to remind us what they're still capable of.
Are we seeing Spurs' best ball of the season? The team at the center of a rankings storm is riding its longest win streak since a seven-gamer this time last season.
It's definitely starting too late to erase Dallas' nine-game division lead, but an eight-game winning streak suggests Spurs' annual second-half push is finally in gear.
Remember back in January when Pop said this was his worst defensive team in years? Since the All-Star break, Spurs have held four teams to season-low point totals.
How unexpected were those back-to-back losses to Bucks and Celts? In their previous 13 games, Spurs were 13-0 and let only five of those 13 foes score more than 82.
Shocker: Spurs have been better in the second half (21-7) than they were in the first half (28-13). It's only happened five seasons out of six this millennium.
It doesn't feel great demoting Spurs after a 19-3 run secured a ninth straight 50-win season, No. 3 all time for such streaks. But Sunday's scores left us no choice.
It's easier said than done, obviously, but Spurs' playoff foes are advised to find a way to score 100 points. SA is 1-10 this season when the opposition hits triple digits.
Two more wins get Spurs to 60. Either way, SA draws the hottest lower seed in Round 1 for the third successive spring: Denver again after Kings and Nuggets previously.

nop.summary: At least one Western Conference upstart out there had shoulders broad enough to handle lofty expectations from the committee. Take notes, Warriors.
The first 4-0 start in the club's 18-season history and being the last team to lose this season, just like that, are memories. Blowing a 27-point lead at Portland will do that.
Hornets got to 4-0 without a real peep from Peja. Now they've rallied from a three-game skid because Peja is starting to look like the great fit we said he'd be.
Playing without D-West and Peja are two big problems. Losing three in a row after winning four in a row, which has already happened twice, might be a bigger problem.
Losing West and Peja would be a killer at any time. But losing both frontcourt starters early is especially rough, with 17 of Hornets' first 30 games on the road.
If you're looking for teams praying Wolves don't get Iverson, the line starts right here, now that Bobby Jax has joined D-West and Peja on the list of unavailables.
You knew going in that injuries would probably settle the last few playoff spots in a brutal West. With Peja and D-West needing surgery, Hornets are living it.
It's not much consolation, but at least Peja, D-West and Hornets aren't alone in their injury misery. Rockets (Yao and T-Mac) can claim to be even more miserable.
Losing Peja, D-West and now Paul is a hideously painful run. But the deeper worry: Peja might have a season-ending back injury to go with that new contract.
Anyone remember that 8-3 start? Injury-ravaged Hornets are 4-18 since . . . and a helpless 1-6 since Paul rolled an ankle, joining Peja and D-West in the sick bay.
First it was a blizzard of season-wrecking injuries, then an actual blizzard. The poor denizens of OKC haven't exactly been rewarded for their fervent Hornets support.
Valid question: After all our fretting about Peja's back prognosis and the painful realities of life without Chris Paul, was David West actually Hornets' key to it all?
Kudos to the never-gets-his-due Byron Scott: Hornets, still waiting for Chris Paul's return, have countered a 4-19 slide and all those injuries by going 6-3 since Jan. 8.
Wouldn't it be something if injury-riddled Hornets, who unraveled late last season, kept rallying all the way back into contention this season now that Paul is back?
Thought I was kidding about Hornets rallying back into playoff contention? They were a gutty 8-10 with Chris Paul out injured and are now in the midst of an 8-2 surge.
Since a 4-19 stretch left them 10 games under .500, Hornets are 13-6. But they're down to their last 11 games in OKC, with 16 more on the road and two in New Orleans.
If the West is so great, how come only six teams have winning records? I'll tell you who doesn't care: Byron Scott's Hornets, who suddenly find themselves at No. 7.
Hornets were 29-23 last season before sliding into the lottery with a 9-21 nosedive. This season? Hoping for the opposite, Hornets are 16-10 since cratering to 12-22.
All those stories about Hornets finishing the season with a flourish to banish the memory of last spring's 9-21 collapse are on hold. They're 0-5 in March.
Paul's reward for putting off the foot surgery he needs? If not for an 18-point comeback in New York on Friday night, his Hornets would be 0-8 in March.
Hornets started 8-3 with Peja playing and should get him back this week. Problem is, it's probably too late unless they win both of their remaining meetings with Clips.
If they don't seem so desperate for No. 8, maybe it's because Hornets have lost 21 games in a row to Dallas. There's no longer active drought in major US team sports.
It seems Peja won't be coming back, after all. Which means that banged-up Hornets' only salvation now might be more overtime games, since they're 6-0 in OT.
Looks like Hornets heard us when they took Clips to OT and improved to 7-0. But it was their only OT game all week and losing the other two ended their season.

uta.summary: This should be fun: Jazz swept Pistons last season as a non-playoff team and play host to them Monday after a start that had made them darlings of scouts everywhere.
Normally we'd make a big fuss about Kirilenko's latest injury, but AK-47 has been only the seventh-leading scorer (8.4 ppg) so far for scorching Utah.
How do we know Jazz are reborn? They just posted a 3-0 week without an injured AK-47 and Sloan is handing big roles to kids like Miles, Brewer and Millsap.
Jazz have been too good, with or without Kirilenko, to drop them after a road loss on a back-to-back. They've been 5-0 good with Kirilenko sitting out, in fact.
You can live with a 1-3 blip after a 12-1 start. Sloan's real issue is giving up two 50-point games in one month, which no NBA team had done since December 1990.
To get that elusive 1,000th victory -- and make the story go away -- all Sloan needs is a Boozer double-double. Jazz are 13-1 when Boozer gets one, 2-4 when he doesn't.
It so easily could (and should) have been a 4-0 week, but it's tough to quibble after a home rout of Dallas, two road wins and with AK-47 still not averaging 10 ppg.
Dare we say Melo's suspension did not clinch Utah's Northwest title by Christmas. Not with Jazz just 8-7 since their 12-1 start and eight of their next 13 on the road.
I know someone who isn't impressed with the five-game Northwest Division lead Jazz are taking into the New Year. Sloan's not afraid to tell them so, either.
Jazz are just 12-9 since their 12-1 start, true, but they still have too many quality victories -- in the face of a tougher sked than most -- to lose their top-five standing.
Make that 12-12 since its 12-1 start and three 50-point games surrendered: Redd, Kobe and now Ray Allen. Hence Utah finally loses its longstanding top-five status.
See? A week at No. 7 did wonders for Utah, just as it did for San Antonio: Jazz respond to their demotion with big road wins at Detroit, Toronto and Chicago.
It's been a painful January by any measure: Jazz are just 7-7 this month after losses to Grizz and Hornets and now Boozer and Kirilenko are carrying injuries.
You usually don't promote teams that just lost their top scorer for a month. But Jazz, after blowing five fourth-quarter leads in January, also just beat Spurs and Suns.
As if their season wasn't sufficiently storybook until now, Okur-led Jazz have won four in a row without Boozer and have knocked Spurs down to fourth in the West.
How did they move up a notch? Jazz are a stunning 6-1 without Boozer, while no other team besides Houston is more than two games over .500 without its leading scorer.
AK-47 and Okur limp off just as Boozer comes back, but this Jazz -- contrary to what we all said coming into the season -- doesn't have to be at full strength to win.
These Jazz have suddenly won four straight roadies, all by double digits, while going 11-2 overall. Plus they're 11-0 in the last 11 games that Deron Williams has played.
That said, you have to strongly consider moving Jazz up. They're on a 13-2 tear and haven't lost a game with Deron Williams healthy since -- yikes -- Jan. 29.
Boozer wound up surviving his long-awaited Cleveland return. But the four-game trip, as an 0-4 whole, represents the low point of Utah's storybook season so far.
As long as Jazz don't surrender HC advantage in Round 1 by letting Rockets pass them in the win column,  they can live with what happens in the rankings. Probably.
Like others before them, Jazz respond to a temporary drop to the cure-all No. 7 spot with a huge win in Houston. Utah is now a tidy 10-4 against the rest of the top six.
Can't decide if Jazz are playin' with fire or swimmin' with sharks, but we do know they're 1-7 in their last eight roadies and just lost at home to Allen-less Sonics.
Difference of opinion: Sloan says this 2-7 slide has ''kind of destroyed a little bit of a great season.'' Owner Larry Miller's view, via the Salt Lake Tribune: Jazz ''suck.''

cle.summary: Honestly? The sight of Sean May rejecting LeBron at the rim -- and then looking down at him with a dismissive glare -- shocked me more than LBJ posterizing Duncan.
No one in the East has a better record, but Cavs' losses to Bobcats and Hawks were a major letdown after their San Antonio breakthrough. They should be 6-0 or 5-1.
These guys are the closest thing we've got to an East beast these days. Of course, until Hughes gets back, Cavs would admit that they really don't qualify, either.
As much as we love the orange unis -- another reason to bring up World B. -- you can't camouflage the fact that Cavs have mostly looked shaky since winning at SA.
I know they miss Hughes. I know nights like Saturday in Houston happen to everyone. But a 6-7 record in the East? With losses to Bobcats, Hawks and Knicks?
Facts are facts: Cavs are 7-2 with Hughes and 5-5 without him. So they welcome a healed Hughes back excitedly, whether or not he's a perfect fit next to LeBron.
It's the so-so effort in this 7-7 stretch that stands out more than the record. Latest example: Cavs fall to slumping Magic on a night Orlando starts Ariza, Battie and Arroyo.
Cavs always say they play better against tougher competition. With 11 of the next 14 on the road, seven of those in the West, this would seem an ideal time to prove it.
Is this is a sign he's turning it up a notch? LeBron scores 30 or more in four of his final six games as a 21-year-old, after a run of seven straight games under 30.
Unlike their previous win over SA, Cavs are building on beating Spurs at home. Can't do much better than a 7-1 surge leading into that dreaded seven-game trip.
Gruesome as Phoenix was, Cavs are thanking Mr. Schedule Maker. They'll wind up playing five of the seven West teams with losing records on this seven-game trip.
The coach was clearly expecting more than a 3-4 trip, judging by Brown saying Cavs should be ''embarrassed and ashamed'' after heavy losses in Seattle and Portland.
Ouch. Just starting out on a stretch with nine of 11 games at home, Cavs have dropped the first three at the Q and watched LeBron pick up a toe injury.
Since going a season-high 10 games over .500, Cavs have dropped eight of 12 ... and their best game in that stretch, strangely, was the one LeBron sat out injured.
Good timing. Amid strong signs LeBron and his coach are clashing over offensive philosophy, Cavs run off three quality home wins: Clips, Heat, Lakers.
The East would have only one 30-win team without Cavs' recent revival. They've been better in the last five games than we've seen all season, including their 7-2 start.
Cavs were crushed that they couldn't swing a Bibby deal. Two defeats since the deadline passed should tell you why they were trying so hard to get one done.
What do you think pleases Cavs more? Ripping Raptors by 23 ... or seeing LeBron shoot 15-for-17 at the line in the win after those crucial late misses in Dallas?
If Cavs keep this 8-3 roll going and snatch No. 1 in the East away from Detroit, LeBron will have a loud last laugh. Maybe he knew what he was doing all along.
No wonder LeBron wants to run more. Cavs are up to 22-3 when they score at least 100 points and they're averaging 103.6 ppg during this eight-game win streak.
Just when it seemed they were pushing for the East's top seed, Cavs post a 1-3 week. Which puts them closer to No. 5 than No. 1, with seven of the next eight on the road.
Cavs won the biggest game of their season Saturday. But they're 3-5 since March 17 and still could slip to No. 5 in the East, which might mean (gulp) Miami in Round 1.
Cavs were the last East team with a shot to finish with a winning record on the road besides Pistons. But Sunday's loss in Detroit ruled out that possibility.
Good gig if you can get it: Larry Hughes will get a $2 million bonus for the second straight season as long as Cavs win 49, even if 49 wins only gets them a No. 5 seed.

det.summary: The only consolation for Pistons after their opening-night debacle -- a small one, granted -- is that all four of last season's final four teams lost their first game.
Life without Big Ben is off to a rocky start: Rip's hurt, Sheed has more Ts (four) than Pistons have wins and you're even starting to hear Etroit jokes. As in no D.
Pistons didn't lose their sixth game last season until Jan. 31. Let's see how long they can delay No. 6 this term after getting Rip back and clawing back to .500.
Pistons certainly haven't beaten any powerhouses during this 6-0 run, but you don't knock an East team on a roll. Not when there's only two of them.
Losing their streak in Charlotte wasn't the best. But Pistons' 11-1 record in six back-to-back sets is quite good, with 16 back-to-backs to go for a league-high 22 overall.
You can't just gloss over losses to Bobcats and Blazers. But you also can't ignore the vintage Dee-troit Bas-ket-ball at Dallas and Orlando in a back-to-back road sweep.
Maybe Pistons should be thankful for their league-high 22 back-to-backs. They're 15-1 in eight back-to-backs so far and -- huh? -- 0-7 in every other game.
This December (7-3) isn't as good as last December (13-2), but Pistons will begin 2007 as the East's current beast, with a still-stingy D and a developing bench.
Maybe they got away with one versus Nets, but Pistons would say things have more than evened out with narrow losses to Knicks and Pacers and Billups' getting hurt.
Pistons can poke fun at Big Ben for Chicago's headband rules all they want, but they look a bit naked themselves without Billups in the midst of a 1-4 rut.
Pistons have to wait until Tuesday before we see any new blood on the roster, but this already looks official: Chauncey is basically irreplaceable. Agreed?
When C-Webb starts, Pistons are 2-0. But it's still disconcerting to see them with just one win against fellow Central Division foes this close to the 41-game midpoint.
Pistons apparently still play DEE-TROIT BAS-KET-BALL on occasion. They're 15-1 when holding teams below 90 ppg and have the East's only winning road record at 13-8.
I know, I know: Pistons already have 18 losses, same as last season. But they care far more about these numbers: Pistons are now 7-3 with Webber and 15-9 on the road.
With Webber, Pistons are 10-3 and look like top-five material again. Best of all, Sheed looks happier than he was partnering any of Big Ben's previous replacements.
Pistons' .627 winning percentage is the second-lowest for any team leading its conference at the break since 1970-71. But their 15-9 road record sparkles.
Pistons are the East's deadline winners. None of their rivals swung a significant deal, either, and snatching up Webber was better than any trade they could've made.
Interesting stretch to register in your datebook: East's best will play Suns, Mavs, Spurs and Rockets from March 16-23, with only one of those games (Dallas) at home.
Losing at home to Warriors and Cavs sounded the alarms anew, but Pistons are still the East's only road juggernaut, starting out 2-0 on their five-game trip out West.
Go figure. Pistons sweep a 5-0 road trip out West, winning the capper in Phoenix despite losing Billups, but are likewise in the midst of a three-game home losing skid.
Pistons are 2-0 when Sheed is serving a techs-induced suspension and just clinched the East's first playoff berth. So they're not stressing about a so-so home record.
Pistons are still the only team in the league better on the road (24-13) than at home (23-13). They'll also be the East's only 50-win team unless Cavs or Bulls get hot.
When Pistons win the Central -- their magic number is two -- it'll be their eighth division title in a span of 20 seasons. Since 1987-88, only Spurs (10) have won more.
Not sure yet if Pistons will finish as the East's lone 50-win club. But we definitely messed up big-time omitting Prince from our list of DPOY candidates. Apologies, Tay.

dal.summary: A few folks in Mavsland warned the committee to expect a slow start from the reigning West champs. Guess they knew what they were talking about.
After a four-game losing streak to end last season and another to start this season, Mavs have actually won two in a row. But they still don't look quite right.
They're still not up to par, not even after five straight Ws, but Nowitzki looks all right. He's got seven double-doubles already, two more than Dirk had all of last November.
Can't ignore the fact that only three victims in Mavs' 9-0 surge have winning records. But don't ignore the fact that Howard missed all but two of those games.
Bold prediction: Mavs won't be going 78-4. Simply matching the club's longest-ever winning streak (14) is two road wins away. But they're an undisputed No. 1, right?
Mavs can deal with a short stay at No. 1. What they're really after is two 20-point scorers every night. Mavs are 7-1 when that happens and 7-5 when it doesn't.
The good news: Howard has averaged 19.6 ppg over the last 10 games. The bad news: Mavs' offense still isn't running smoothly, so Nowitzki needs more help.
Dirk's latest ankle scare looked bad on TV, but Mavs weren't too worried. Besides that outside game for the ages, our favorite 7-footer is also blessed with bionic ankles.
Cowboys have, what, one significant W in the Romo Era? The real title contender in town, meanwhile, rolls along with zero hoopla, even at 24-3 since that 0-4 start.
When you've stamped yourselves as the NBA's clear-cut No. 1, as Mavs have, you have to have at least two All-Stars. Howard must go to Vegas with Dirk, end of story.
As if a 31-4 record since that 0-4 start isn't gaudy enough, check this out: Dirk is shooting .525 and averaging 30.8 ppg since switching back to the leather ball.
Unlike last season's Pistons, who might have peaked at 36-5, Mavs appear to be getting stronger, sitting just three wins shy of their third double-digit win streak.
It's a rough world out there: Mavs have played .917 ball since Dec. 13, winning 22 of 24 in that span, yet can't really hit us with a protest that they've slipped to No. 2.
25-2 since Dec. 11, 15 straight wins at home, 27-6 vs. West teams ... and swimming in fresh vengeance fuel after Josh Howard's omission as an All-Star reserve.
As you'd imagine, Mavs are the toast of their town. But you can safely assume they weren't consulted on Cowboys' coaching hire when it goes to a guy named Wade.
We're going to let you in on a little secret: You've got to score at least 92 points to have any chance against Mavs. They're 22-0 when holding teams to 91 or fewer.
The big winners at the deadline? It might have been those pesky Mavs, who began the week on a 32-2 run and saw none of their nearest rivals make an impact trade.
Yet another streak to track: Mavs are 11-0 in the second game of back-to-backs, with five to go. No team has ever finished a season losing fewer than two such games.
If you just added up their three longest winning streaks -- 12, 13 and the current 17-gamer -- Mavs  still would have a higher win total than all but three other teams.
Mavs' first losing streak since their 0-4 start in November left them on a 68-14 pace. But we repeat: Who around Dallas really took advantage? Right, nobody.
Mavs are a mere 6-0 since Suns loss, but Dirk senses you're not impressed: ''We win 17 in a row, lose one game and . . . everybody says we're nothing.'' Not us, pal.
Actual quote from Dirk after Mavs were denied a single-season record fourth double-digit win streak: ''Are we down to No. 2?'' He seemed strangely surprised to hear no.
After those gaudy records they posted in January (14-2), February (10-0) and March (12-2), I don't quite know how to react to Mavs sitting at a mere 2-2 in April.
Only twice since 2000 has the team with the best record won it all. But you figure Mavs will take their chances after one of the most extraordinary regular seasons ever.

mia.summary: Didn't expect them to stay up here long, not after winning it all without ever reaching No. 1. But I didn't expect Heat to lose interest by halftime on Opening Night.
Second half vs. Sonics. Second half in New Jersey. So make that two glimpses of Miami's ''on'' switch to go with two ugly home losses (Chicago and now Houston).
The two Shaq-sized issues here: How much will keeping this team afloat without Shaq take out of Wade and Co. for later? And what will Shaq look like when he's back?
Shaq's rookie season is the only full, non-lockout season in his career in which his team failed to win 50 games. Anyone else getting the feeling that this'll be No. 2?
For all the talk about how little help D-Wade's getting with Shaq out, Heat really can't ask for more from Haslem, who's averaging a healthy 13.4 ppg and 9.7 rpg.
Heat have quietly won four of their past six games, three of those coming on the road, and somehow begin the new week at No. 8 in the East. What a conference.
Since we know Shaq's out for Christmas, here's a more pertinent question: How long before Miami beats someone with a winning record? None of its 10 victims has one.
Shaq-less Heat are 8-9 since Prof. Hollinger proclaimed them a candidate to plummet all the way into the lottery ... but just a half-game out of a playoff spot.
News flash: If D-Wade can't shake this wrist thing fairly soon, Shaq needn't rush back. Heat's title defense, without those two, would be over before the playoffs start.
Wade returns and, just like that, Riley-less Heat no longer look like an expansion team. Including the game he left early, Heat are 0-6 without Wade, 14-13 with him.
Maybe Heat are trying their hardest to convince Riley to rush back from hip  surgery . . . or maybe this 4-1 trip simply proves they feel liberated by Riles' absence.
If Lakers can start 11-19 in '02-03 thanks to a Shaq injury and still finish 50-32, you can understand why Shaq and his Heat never really panicked in this East.
Shaq's return hasn't exactly inspired the champs, who are 0-3 since, but Heat haters should note that Miami arguably has the East's easiest remaining schedule.
Heat look a lot more serious since surrendering 52 points to Knicks' Crawford. Maybe that woke up the champs like their big loss in Dallas around this time last season.
Thanks to a 6-1 surge, Heat can actually reach .500 by the All-Star break -- for the first time since the champs were 3-3 -- if they win their only game this week.
The stars are aligning: Riley returns to rejoin Shaq and Wade. Heat, meanwhile, will play 15 of their final 25 games at home after a tough finish to February.
Only one champion since 1970 -- Chicago after MJ's 1998 retirement -- has failed to reach the playoffs in the following season. But my bet is Heat won't be No. 2.
Didn't see that coming: Heat rebound from their annual regular-season rout in Dallas with maybe their best four-game stretch of the season ... all of it without D-Wade.
That's 12 wins in a row at home, 14 of 18 overall and suddenly Heat, in spite of all those injuries, look like they're lining up a last laugh as loud as LeBron's.
Maybe we shouldn't be so surprised that Heat turned it on now, even without Wade. Miami is 40-2 at home in February and March since Shaq arrived in the '04-05 season.
First a 25-point loss to unraveling Indy? Then a 19-point blown lead at home to Philly? Yes, Mr. Wade. Heat were 11-3 without you, but they're ready for you now.
Trivia time: How many times this season have Heat dressed their top eight players and their head coach? Answer: Once. The night D-Wade went down in Houston.
If the current seedings hold, Heat would face Cavs in Round 1 and Pistons in Round 2. Hardly ideal, but I suspect Cleveland and Detroit won't be any happier about it.
Who would defending champs rather see in Round 1? Few would have predicted this before the season, but it's certainly true now: LeBron's Cavs over Chicago.

lac.summary: More evidence it's a new day in Clipperland: Dunleavy's lads suffered one understandable loss in three games and folks are still asking What's wrong?
I'm eager to take in Clips' challengng trip Tuesday to Utah, just their second roadie all season, because their home games -- no joke -- have been too easy lately.
They're not worried about the 0-2 start on the road. They're too busy worrying about what's wrong with Kaman, who looks nothing like a $50-some million player.
Respect around town and how they stack up with their co-tenants can't be priorities now. Not when they're 0-5 away from Staples, sinking Clips to last in the Pacific.
East aside, this is November's most disappointing team. Routing Orlando doesn't change the fact that Clips are 0-6 on the road and have sunk to last in the Pacific.
Clips are no longer the only team without a road W after conquering Memphis. But no team that started 0-7 on the road has reached the playoffs since Suns in '96-97.
The argument against Iverson: Clips have played only three games vs. East teams. The argument for A.I.: Mired in a 4-11 funk, do Clips have much chemistry to lose?
Didn't expect Clips to go after Artest again so soon. But it's not so shocking when their defense, an oft-overlooked key last season, has dropped off so drastically.
Funny how that works. Clips finally hook up with a couple East teams (Celts and Knicks) and suddenly have their first three-game win streak since starting 5-1.
Remember when we said that nothing less than 50 wins would do? With their less-than-sterling road record of 3-13, Clips now need a 35-13 finish to get there.
The lackluster play has lasted so long that you have to wonder: Do Clips have to make a trade so everyone on the team will stop waiting for one?
All the Maggette trade chatter obscures the fact that Clips, who still find themselves adrift of playoff range, have only one win over a winning team since Christmas.
With the help of a 4-1 homestand, Clips claw back to .500. But they've got just six road wins in 20 tries, with a seven-game trip through the East starting Friday.
Since stumbling to a bad loss in Atlanta on Jan. 6, Clips are 9-4. The next five games, all roadies in the East, should tell us if this is going to be a lasting recovery.
Attention, Clips: Just make sure that, at the very least, you get to 89 points. You're 0-13 when you score 88 points or less ... and 25-13 in all the other games.
They haven't exactly sunk to the depth of your father's Clippers, but these Clips have to pull out a playoff berth just to shed their Most Disappointing Team tag.
With the trade deadline passing, Maggette rumors are officially on hold. Of course, that also means Clips can no longer use Maggette's situation as a distraction alibi.
Clips can still make the playoffs without Livingston, sure. But a key component of their future has now dislocated both of his knees in his first three pro seasons.
If this is their playoff push, Clips better start pushing a lot harder. They're 1-4 in March after getting routed at home by Sheed-less Pistons, yet to score 90 this month.
No wonder they've sunk out of the West's top eight. Clips have won just once in their past eight road games and just twice in their nine games this month.
The secret to finishing eighth? Even sans Cassell, banged-up Clips are now 5-0 in one-point games after winning in MIL . . . and after just one one-point W last season.
Surest sign yet that Clips have righted their slip and will reach the playoffs, with or without Cassell: Friday's victory was L.A.'s first in 18 games in Sacramento since 1997.
Pertinent question we might as well start considering now: If Clips hang onto a playoff spot sans Cassell and Livingston, who replaces them as Most Disappointing Team?
After back-to-back seasons with the best record in town, Clips can no longer make it three. They can't even make the playoffs now without help from Golden State.

lal.summary: After a nightmarish preseason, who saw this coming? They're 1-1 with Kobe playing and 2-0 with Odom, Bynum, Turiaf and Walton running the operation.
Lakers have to capitalize on that favorable early schedule, but there's a catch: Kobe says it'll be ''January or February'' before he's at full strength.
Lots to be thankful for indeed. Kobe's recovering, Bynum's blossoming and Lakers are only four games (3-1) into a stretch where they play 13 of 14 at Staples Center.
Who needs a smooth training camp? Lakers continue to make the most of this home-heavy early schedule and, as a bonus, sent Clippers into a spiral.
As stated last week: Who needs a smooth training camp? Not Kobe, who's shooting a career-best 49 percent from the floor and hushing all that It's A Clipper Town stuff.
We repeat: Who needs a smooth training camp? Kobe's Lakers couldn't have finished their forever stay at Staples (16 of 20 games) any stronger, roughing Spurs up.
Lakers can only hope folks are right when they say this team can handle an Odom injury better than ever. Since Odom arrived, L.A. is 92-76 with him, 4-19 without him.
You were wrong if you figured Lakers would fold or Kobe would just fire away with Odom out. L.A. is 4-3 sans Lamar and Bryant has averaged 7.8 apg over the last five.
Phil has said plenty about Kwame lately, but make no mistake. Lakers need him back from Sunday's ankle sprain ASAP, only 10 games (5-5) into life without Odom.
Credit where credit is due: Lakers haven't had Lamar for either of their meetings with Mavs and still matched up with the team in the top spot as well as anyone we've seen.
Did they get too much credit? After halting Mavs' 13-game win streak minus Odom and Kwame, how did Lakes go to Memphis and Houston and lose by 10 and 25?
Recent losses to Bobcats, Grizz and now Hornets are even tougher to explain when you see that Lakes are 10-4 against the other seven teams in the West's top eight.
Going 12-9 without Odom -- with 13 of those games on the road -- was impressive. Getting swept by Bobcats and losing twice to banged-up Hornets, not so much.
Kobe gets suspended! Kobe hears an MVP chant in Boston! Kobe grills Arenas! Kobe seethes seeing LeBron avoid suspension! And this crazy trip is only half over.
It was Lakers' longest trip since 1989 and it didn't start or end well. The bookends on this 3-5 jaunt: Kobe's one-game suspension and a three-game losing streak.
Walton was Lakers' second-best player with Odom out and they miss him more than anyone anticipated. Starting with the night he got hurt, L.A. is 3-9 without Luke.
At 23-11, Kobe was an MVP candidate and the Zenmeister was COY material. But Lakers' recent slide reached 7-14 before weekend wins over Celts and Warriors.
Let's be realistic, shall we? With Odom out indefinitely and Walton still sidelined, how much can Pippen really help Lakers ... even if he's somehow spry at 41?
Lakers are due for some good news after a 3-12 slide and Kobe's second suspension . . . and here it is: Lamar Odom says he expects to be back this week.
What a conference. Lakers endure separate six- and seven-game skids in a six-week span but still cling to the No. 6 seed, even in the (allegedly) mighty West.
The funny thing about Kobe's 53.6 ppg average during this historic run? Lakers have needed every point, only winning those five games by an average of 4.4.
Lakers are 20-8 when Kobe is joined by these three bigs in the lineup: Odom, Walton and Kwame Brown. But with so many injuries, Kobe's Lakers are just 19-23 in 2007.
The current 2-5 slump, with all five of the losses at Staples, would be causing more of a panic if Lakers didn't want to finish with the No. 7 seed and face Suns in Round 1.
This won't be the first losing season in Phil Jackson's career. But it is Phil's first-ever losing record since the All-Star break: 11-16 in spite of all those 50s from Kobe.

bkn.summary: Nets' start is best summed up by two words: Weird scheduling. They'll play only four games in the season's first 11 days . . . with two of those against Miami.
The only team out there to beat Utah can't exactly celebrate. Not after dropping to 0-2 against Miami just two nights later and losing Jefferson indefinitely.
Not a lot of mystery here. Hard to imagine New Jersey getting swept at home by the league's Pacific Northwest chapter, in the space of six days, if RJ were healthy.
Don't think this was the sort of consistency Nets were going for, but a 5-8 start falls right in line with last season's 9-12 start, 2-11 in '04-05 and 7-11 in '03-04.
Figures. After my recent ode to J-Kidd in the Weekend Dime, he fails to score in double figures six times in seven games, five of them losses.
The lesson from that epic loss to Phoenix? Push the pace, Nets. They're (ugh) 1-9 when held below 100 points, which only adds to L-Frank's increasing woes.
Couldn't beat Bosh-less Raps. Sub-.500 even at home. With 10 of 15 January games on the road, Nets overcoming their annual slow start might be tougher than ever.
Overcoming their seemingly annual slow start is no lock now, with Krstic lost for the season and Jefferson ailing, too. So you have to ask: time to shop Vince/start over?
Even without Krstic, Nets still have enough to win the Titanic . . . if Vince does more than we've seen in the past 10 games, six of them under the 20-point plateau.
Nets'  3-1 rebound is just a start. They're still at -6, second worst in East plus/minus behind Charlotte, when adding up their road wins (four) and home losses (10).
After their 5-2 rebound, Nets play 11 of their next 15 on the road. Yet you suspect they won't mind the part about getting some distance from the NYC tabloid circus.
You'd think that Jefferson finally conceding he needs surgery would have Nets freaked, but look at Nets' response to Kidd's personal crisis: 9-2 since Dec. 27.
Trivia time: Nets are just the fourth team in history to suffer three consecutive losses by a single point, joining Pacers (1999), Lakers (1995) and Bulls (1987).
If they don't end up winning the worst division in creation, it'll probably be because Nets have to be leading the league in excruciating, heart-ripped-out losses.
Coach Frank, they say, is safe. Kidd and/or Vince? Sounds like we won't be able to say for sure for another 10 days. Until the trade deadline passes, in other words.
Interesting hypothetical: If Nets hadn't lost seven games already this season by two points or less, would we be hearing so much Kidd/Carter trade talk?
If they're unhappy to be stuck in Jersey, it's tough to tell. Since the trade buzzer sounded: Kidd had a triple-double, Carter had a 40-point game and Nets are 2-0.
Let's go out on a limb and suggest that any momentum Nets had after deciding not to trade Kidd or Carter is gonzo after back-to-back losses to Celts and Sixers.
If current form holds, Nets' worst nightmare will be realized: Knicks would claim the East's final playoff spot and send New Jersey to Secaucus for the draft lottery.
Since they (predictably) went 0-3 on their Texas Triangle trip, losing by an average of 16.7 ppg, Nets are 3-1 with reactivated Jefferson leading them in scoring twice.
Common sense says Nets vets are the most likely group out there to fall upwards into a playoff berth. But only one word can describe their recent play: Lackluster.
Falling upwards remains the most accurate description for Nets' playoff ''drive.'' They awoke Monday sitting seventh in the East despite a 6-9 record in March.
Jefferson said recently that Nets had a four-game win streak left in them. If so, it'll include at least one W over their neighbors, with Knicks still on the schedule twice.
Nets not only can still sneak up to a sixth seed in the season's final hours, but a 2-0 finish would quietly give the much-maligned Titanic two teams at .500 or better.

phx.summary: Opening up 4-5 last season, that was a bad start. Blowing big leads on the road (Lakers) and at home (Utah) adds up to a full-fledged worrying start.
If Saturday night's 25-point, 14-board Amare sticks around for a while, I'm guessing Suns will say a 1-5 start was a worthy sacrifice.
D'Antoni says Nash's latest back woes aren't costing him any sleep. If it gets to the sleep-deprivation point, though, it won't even matter how Amare's coming along.
Suns aren't just starting to heat up. They're 6-1 since a 1-5 start and they're starting to get Amare, Diaw and Matrix on the court. Together. As a frontcourt trio.
After Amare rumbles for at least 20-and-10 in four straight games, I think even the skeptics would agree: You'd welcome an 80-percent Amare on your team.
Five straight double-doubles for Nash, seven in eight games for Amare and three seasons in a row that Suns have had a win streak of at least 10 games. Ho hum.
Just a hunch, but I'm guessing no one will protest too loudly about Suns retaining the No. 1 spot for a second successive week. Not even from Salt Lake City.
Considering the travel hell they endured just to make it to their first loss in five weeks and the show they put on in defeat, Suns deserve to stay at No. 1. Don't they?
Here's why a 15-game win streak is big no matter who Suns played: 15 teams in this league, including all five in the Atlantic, don't even have 15 wins yet.
Dropping to 0-2 against Dallas didn't exactly ruin them. Suns are 6-0 since and 24-3 overall since their 1-5 start, with only one loss to a team outside our top eight.
What's wilder? Suns going 27-3 since that 1-5 start? Or Suns establishing a 64-18 pace and still trailing Mavs by 1 ½ games for the league's best record?
How hot are they? Suns have lost all of two games in two months and are a mere
We'd make a bigger deal about Suns' alleged struggles vs. Jazz, Spurs and Lakers if their four losses to those teams hadn't come so early, all before Thanksgiving.
Dropping to 0-3 vs. Utah is undeniably disconcerting, but not as troubling for Suns as facing 35 more games with a seven-man rotation and injuries starting to crop up.
Has everyone seen enough in the past week to forever bury that ridiculous ''Nash can't be the MVP because he plays with too many All-Stars'' argument? Thanks.
Can't wait to see how the Nash-bashers spin this one: Suns promptly lose three in a row without him and fall to 4-12 over the past three seasons when he's injured.
Nash returns, Suns post a 4-0 week and Charles Barkley annoys his former employers with his TV criticism. Sounds like things are getting back to normal in the desert.
Still not quite sure how they scored just 94 points to lose in Philly, even without Marion, but Suns continue to look more like themselves again at 7-1 with Nash back.
Even at 9-1 since the break, D'Antoni is the first to admit Spurs are playing better ball. But Suns ain't going to drop far with 17 more road wins than home losses.
Suns follow up their most impressive victory of the season by losing both games of a back-to-back by a combined 46 points? That's what you call a Letdown Effect.
Suns just clinched their third straight division title after winning only three from 1968-2004. One caution: Suns' lead over Spurs for the No. 2 seed is down to three games.
Suns are only 6-4 in their last 10 games. But when two of those Ws come against one of the foremost regular-season juggernauts of all time, committees like us notice.
Seems like Spurs aren't Suns' only problem at present. Says Nash: ''The chemistry's not great. . . . We're a little bit selfish. We're a little bit woe-is-me right now.''
Fast fact: Suns have three 60-win seasons in club history and the PG for two of them was Nash. Bonus plan: A stress-free week awaits with the No. 2 seed clinched.

chi.summary: After torching Miami, Bulls should have flown in Kareem to give the same speech he gave Magic after his first NBA game: Stop celebrating. There are 81 more of these.
Offensively challenged Bulls need more consistency from Ben ... Ben Gordon, that is. Gordon's wacky scoring totals in the first six games: 6, 24, 5, 37, 2, 3.
A handy alibi if they want it: Bulls' annually dreaded circus road trip is a seven-gamer that began with three in Texas. No surprise, though: Skiles doesn't want it.
With a soft stretch coming, Bulls can rally like they did the last two seasons, from 12-19 and 0-9. Tougher to call: Will the first Skiles-Big Ben spat fade or mushroom?
Bulls have endured the hardest schedule in the league so far, as well as a national headband debate, but none of that really has set them back. What a conference.
An easier schedule certainly helped, but it was still impressive to see Bulls respond to Headbandgate with a 7-0 burst in which they averaged (no joke) 106.4 ppg.
Knicks, Nuggets and the league office are praying their scandal fades as fast as Headbandgate. Amid much chaos elsewhere, Big Ben snares 62 boards in three wins.
A cushy schedule accelerated Bulls' 13-2 run, but Gordon's move to the bench hasn't hurt. Back as sixth man for 21 games, Gordon has led the team in scoring 10 times.
He might not like it, but this is why Bulls have to do what's best for them and use Gordon as a sixth man: Little Ben has scored 20 or more in 11 of his last 12 games.
No letup from Bulls against Chauncey-less Pistons, but two bad fourth quarters -- against Suns, then Nets -- cost Chicago what could have been a 3-0 week.
When does a 111-66 win feel empty? When A) you're playing Memphis and B) you've lost five of the previous six games, having blown big leads in four of them.
Bulls are 4-6 in 2007, which is why Gordon has been moved back into the starting lineup ... even though five of those losses were inflicted by first-place teams.
After a 1-5 start to the New Year, Bulls are back in the top 10 (where they belong) with a 6-2 spurt that includes impressive home victories over Spurs and Mavs.
After Ben Gordon's East snub, Bulls still haven't had an All-Star since MJ retired in 1998. And Skiles, who loves being the unappreciated underdog, still doesn't mind.
Compared to their last seven-game trip, on which they went 1-6 -- and 0-5 against West foes -- Bulls will get a pass from Skiles for going 3-4 on this one. Maybe.
Bulls' 1-5 skid into the break is just one element of a frustrating February. Of the 12 teams that didn't have an All-Star, only Chicago has a winning record.
Bulls are subjected to more trade rumors than anyone this side of KG, so we probably shouldn't be surprised that they've looked sharper and more settled post-deadline.
Is Gordon finally more dangerous as a starter than he was as a sixth man? Hard to argue when he's pumping in 48 on the road to keep pace with Our Favorite Lefty.
Wednesday's return to South Florida didn't quite work out like Opening Night, but Bulls are a healthy 8-3 since the All-Star break in spite of that 33-point debacle in Miami.
Bulls are destined for the East's No. 5 seed, but remember: They'll have home-court advantage in the first round as long as they have more wins than the No. 4 seed.
Skiles was predictably enraged by that one-point loss at Memphis, but Bulls' last three Ws in an 8-3 month came by four points combined. Can't win every close one.
Even though Chicago has given Miami fits on a playoff stage, I'll go out on a limb and suggest Bulls would rather pass Cavs if they can to secure an easier first-round foe.
The way Bulls are going, at 17-7 since the All-Star break and 12-4 against fellow Central tenants, they haven't backed into the No. 2 seed. They've deservedly risen.
A win Wednesday over Nets gives Bulls their first 50-win season since MJ's Bulls went 62-20 in 1997-98 . . . and no Pistons, Heat or Cavs until the conference finals.

mil.summary: You know us. Winning in Detroit on Opening Night was a big team step . . . but all we really care about is our man Redd shredding Pistons for 37.
When you lose five of six after an opening night W at Detroit -- and when 57 points from my favorite lefty don't add up to a win -- you deserve a steep drop.
Simmons is still out, Villanueva just joined him and Bucks are 0-1 when Redd tops 50. Guess we weren't wrong when we doubted they'd match last season's 17-11 start.
Rhetorical question alert: If Bucks can keep taking double-digit leads without Villanueva and Simmons, shouldn't they be able to hold one or two without them?
Toughest week so far begins with news that Simmons might be out for the season. The response? Bucks stun Lakers and Warriors on the road and scare Suns, too.
Honestly? When I checked Bucks' record and saw they were only four games under .500, I was a bit surprised. With the injuries and such, it feels like more.
Charlie V.'s still not right, but at least Bucks have won four straight at home, with the self-proclaimed Kobe Stopper (Patterson) averaging 16.7 ppg and 6.9 rpg in Dec.
With Redd getting scoring help from Mo Williams and Bucks winning six straight at home, Central is finally starting to live up to its top-to-bottom reputation for quality.
It was Redd's trimester -- you can't convince me otherwise -- but December also belonged to Mo Williams: 19.9 ppg, 6.6 apg, 5.8 rpg and 48.9-percent shooting.
Ugh. Missing time with a knee injury, after all the other injuries in Milwaukee this season, is not how we wanted to see our man Redd prove how valuable he is.
With Redd, Villanueva, Simmons and now Mo Williams all sidelined by injury, you could call them Hornets East. Which isn't what Bucks were going for, obviously.
Bucks' only victory in five games since Boykins arrived required 30 points from Little Earl. Redd and Mo Williams, in other words, can't get back to work soon enough.
The good news: Redd is due back about a week before the All-Star break. The bad news: Banged-up Bucks are 2-9 without him and just 2-11 in 2007.
Redd's back this week to swing back at East coaches who spurned him. Which isn't so far-fetched: Bucks are 11-9 when Redd, Mo Williams, Villanueva are all in the lineup.
Bucks are now 3-16 sans Redd, who criminally has no All-Star berth to rush back for. I'm still so mad about the snub that I don't blame him for taking extra time to heal.
As our favorite lefty returns, it's worth repeating that Bucks were an absolute mess without him, going 3-17 sans Redd to drop into the league's bottom five record-wise.
Bucks came out of the break with 19 of their final 29 games at home. It would've been the league's kindest stretch run if Redd's injury hadn't already KO'd them.
A fun little stat, unless you happen to work for Milwaukee: Bucks dropped to 1-11 against Central Division opposition after my beloved Redd's 52 couldn't top Bulls.
Redd after Bucks fell to 0-2 when he scores a half-century: ''I don't think it's good for me to score 50 any more.'' You can't imagine how much it hurts us to hear that.
At the time of the coaching change, Bucks had the league's worst record in 2007 at 7-26 . . . 2-15 on the road. Boston, by comparison, was 9-26, with Memphis at 9-25.
Bogut and Villanueva done for the year. Bucks' seven-game homestand is done, too. So routing Spurs in his debut figures to be Krystkowiak's highlight for a while.
With 15 losses in 16 road games, Bogut and Villanueva done for the season and our man Redd taking precautionary nights off, Worst in the East status is still within reach.
Krystkowiak is excused for losses now because it helps Bucks' draft odds. But fixing the D is job No. 1 next season: It has held only three teams under 90 points.
It had to be painful going 5-22 without Redd and slumping to the league's third-worst record. But it won't sting nearly as much if injury-riddled Bucks land a top-three pick.

hou.summary: Rockets are 1-1 in their division after going 1-15 vs. Southwest last season. But just when T-Mac's back seems fine, his new problem (free throws) persists.
JVG has been saying T-Mac's greatest strength is his decision-making. Judging by T-Mac's 6.4 apg and Yao's early dominance, perhaps they're all in agreement.
First Brad Lidge's ERA soared and now Rockets can't close games. But before you exaggerate the problem, let's not forget Houston did rout Dallas and Miami.
Van Gundy speaks out against the ''Rocket hate'' he keeps hearing. But I'm guessing he'll gradually be able to tune it out if Yao and T-Mac can win nine of every 13.
Rough week for T-Mac, who took painful shots to the hip and the head, but a healthy month for Rockets, who enjoyed their first 10-win November since 1996-97.
Rockets aren't getting too carried away with their fine start. Not with four other teams in the West playing .700 ball, Phoenix right there and T-Mac's back ailing anew.
T-Mac's back isn't Rockets' only sore spot. It's safe to say they're in no rush to see Lakers again after L.A. teased them twice and won both times in a four-day span.
Rockets spank Spurs without T-Mac, helped big by Bonzi, only for Yao to go down one night later. Didn't have the heart to drop 'em, but it'll soon be unavoidable.
In the event T-Mac's back has somehow been cured by that new specialist -- assuming chronic back woes can be cured -- maybe Yao's latest setback isn't a crisis.
Rockets were 6-10 minus Yao last season. But they're 5-3 this time, with T-Mac scoring 31 or more for five straight and Mutombo at 13.8 rpg in the same span.
OK, OK. If you're going to exclude the game in which Yao played just six minutes and got hurt, Rockets have only two Ls (in 11 games) without him, not three.
Even for these experts in pain, Rockets' latest succession of body blows -- T-Mac's tweaked back and the home fold to Denver to seal an 0-3 week -- was torture.
Texas has a truly fearsome triangle going when Houston, which was 16-11 with Yao, can maintain its push for a top-four seed by going 11-5 without him.
Our bad. Rockets should've been ahead of Wiz even before Wiz lost Jamison, with Houston sweeping the season series and now somehow up to 13-7 without Yao.
How can Rockets be 16-11 with Yao and 16-7 without him? T-Mac is still scorching and their defense is No. 1 in ppg allowed (90.4) and defensive FG pct. (42.2).
Rockets are 17-8 without Yao, 2-5 without T-Mac and 14-6 when both are healthy. Now to see if all that adds up to the first taste of the second round for this duo.
Last season, Rockets were riddled with injuries and won 34 games. This season, with Yao and T-Mac together in only 20 games, Rockets have topped that total already.
Proud as they are to be 20-12 without Yao, Rockets have lost five of their last eight games. In other words, they'll be relieved to see him back in the lineup Monday.
No one has noticed because the four teams above them in the West are winning so much, but Yao scored 37 in his fourth game back and Rockets are 3-1 in those four.
Our apologies: Rockets' season finale at Utah should have made our top 25 games list Friday, with home-court advantage in the first round potentially on the line.
Rockets are 8-3 with Yao back and have held 25 opponents to 85 points or fewer. Those are two variables in a formula adding up to a win total that would lead the East.
This could still be the first T-Mac team to get past Round 1, but chances are it won't be the first T-Mac team to have home-court advantage. Not after that Utah loss.
Despite losing three in a row at home -- first one to Utah, even -- and briefly losing T-Mac and Yao, Rockets are right there for a shot at home-court advantage in Round 1.
It's not just T-Mac and Yao: The franchise hasn't won a series since 1997. But this will be the first time since '97 that Rockets have home-court advantage in Round 1.

was.summary: Arenas told us he's ''going to do a documentary on myself . . . just to see how quirky I really am.'' Isn't wearing a boxing robe to the home opener a decent hint?
It's been just a so-so start for Wiz, but our first check of Arenas' rebound from the free-throw line is promising. He's shooting a tidy 92.5 percent, 49 for 53.
The less said about those gold jerseys, the better. The bigger issue: Does Gil have to score 40 for Wiz to win? They're 3-0 when he does, 1-5 when he doesn't.
At 0-7, Wiz share the league's worst road record with young Raps and injury-ravaged Grizz. But you expect that from Raps and Grizz. Not an alleged East contender.
Arenas has been held to 10 points or less three times . . . and Wiz are still the East's (and the league's) worst road team at 0-8. It's bizarre, not quirky.
Much, much better. Wiz throttled Dallas, won their first two roadies (in a row, even) and finally saw some consistency from Arenas (four straight games of 30-plus).
Butler has been playing All-Star ball from the jump. The real change in this 8-2 rebound is obviously the production/steadiness coming from Captain Quirk.
Go ahead, use 'em all: Agent Zero, Captain Quirk, World's Greatest Arenas. Ring up 60 and 54 in a six-day span, as Gil did, and one nickname isn't enough.
Wiz fans should be thanking me for picking Redd over Arenas for East MVP of Trimester 1. We all know Arenas lives off snub fuel and he'll surely be inhaling this.
The shocker is not that Wiz finally lost in Toronto after a 10-2 surge. The shocker is that Gil, averaging 46.4 ppg in those gaudy gold jerseys, had only 33.
Don't really want to believe there's a connection, but the numbers make you wonder: Arenas is shooting .310 from the floor (23 for 74) since his birthday extravaganza.
The good news for Gil's long-shot MVP hopes: Wiz are tied for the East's best record. The bad news: Even at No. 1 in the Least, Wiz are only on pace to finish 49-33.
No one expected these guys to lead the East at any stage, but credit where credit is due: Wiz are 22-8 since their 4-9 start and 9-5 since starting 0-8 on the road.
I was wrong: Simmons did write Wiz would win their division before the season began. Yet I think we'd all agree Wiz better see a swift return from Jamison to stay there.
The coach is exactly right. Great as he is, Gil's obsession with hanging 50 on Portland was doubly inappropriate with Jamison out and teammates brawling anew.
Wiz have done more feuding than winning lately, at 2-4 without Jamison, but sending their coaches to Vegas says to me that they've exceeded a lot of expectations.
The Florida teams would be grateful, at this point, just to snag a playoff berth. Wiz, in other words, are a virtual lock to win their division now unless Arenas goes down.
Arenas thanks refs for Sunday's win over Warriors ... but he's even more thankful about the weekend reactivations of Jamison (Wiz were 4-8 without him) and Butler.
You can just see it coming. With 12 of their final 20 games on the road, Wiz are bound to lose their division lead . . . and still have to face hated Heat in Round 1.
The good news: Wiz are 5-3 in March after a 4-7 February. The bad news: Hanging onto their Southeast Division lead just got a lot tougher now that Butler's ailing.
The good Gilbert: Arenas' layup as time expired in Seattle marked his third buzzer-beating game winner of the season. No one else in the league has more than one.
The division title was slipping away from Wiz even with Butler healthy. But losing the Wisconsin native in Milwaukee, probably 'til next season, was needlessly cruel.
It brings us no joy to heap more misery on Wiz, but the reality is that they were slipping before Butler and Arenas went down, going just 11-15 in February and March.
Every year you hear of the Team No One Wants To Play in Round 1. Meet this spring's banged-up opposite, with Wiz close to going sub-.500 for first time since 10-11.

phi.summary: Guess this also isn't the season that Iverson, now 31, slows down. AI and new sixth man Korver have been deadly in one of the most surprising starts anywhere.
With the For Sale sign removed and the team yanked off the market, it's only natural to ask: Does this mean Iverson is going back on the market?
Webber, just to clarify, was registering his unhappiness when he sounded off last week, not demanding a trade. He surely knows Sixers tried all summer to move him.
If that 3-0 start proves to be a mirage, it won't be Iverson's fault. He's topped 30 points six times this season . . . with 10-plus assists in four of those games.
Anyone remember that 3-0 start, which included a win at Orlando? If it feels like forever ago, that's because Sixers have only two wins in the 27 days since.
So what will happen first? A win to snap the league's longest active losing streak? Or an Iverson trade? Answer is ... you tell us. But we're leaning toward the W.
Iverson might be fuming in exile, but I'm guessing he's happier than his ex-mates, who'd look like '72-73's Sixers (1-19 after 20 games) if not for that 3-0 start.
Two wins in a row after two W's in (gulp) 44 days. But we repeat our Weekend Dime warning: Miller, Smith could make Sixers just decent enough to hurt their Oden odds.
This seven-game trip out West comes at a good time for Sixers fans rooting for extra ping-pong balls in the lottery. Not an easy place to find post-trade momentum.
So much for a spell of calm after a year (or is that years?) on Iverson Trade Alert. Sixers can expect When Will Larry Replace Mo? questions every day now.
Sixers have played a league-low 13 games at home. Of course, given what the roster looks like these days, you don't hear many Philly folks pining for them.
76ers still have the East's worst record, but for how much longer? Celts and sprialing Hawks seem determined to keep Philly just out of Oden-Durant territory.
Don't say we didn't warn you: Miller-led Sixers have just won three of four and have only 12 road games left after January, none of which helps their Oden-Durant odds.
It's nothing Sixers can really celebrate if the goal is scoring a top-two pick, but it is a fact: Philly is 10-15 since trading Iverson, no worse than Denver's 9-13 mark.
You'd have to say it's still AI's team. Since Sixers bottomed out at 10-29, Iguodala has led them in scoring 12 times in 13 games, with Philly going 7-6 in that span.
After this week's obligations, Sixers close with 16 of their final 26 games at home. You figure that'll cost them a few more Ping Pong balls in the lottery.
Back-to-back heavy losses to Bobcats and Bucks suggest (to us, anyway) that Sixers finally realized they were winning a little too often for their own (draft-day) good.
With their first four-game win streak since Dec. 2005 -- and with Andre Iguodala as leading scorer every time -- Sixers are up to 17-20 since trading away the original AI.
The East's hottest team moved up this high in part by default. But Sixers better keep winning and make playoffs now, given their dwindling odds for a top-two pick.
Sixers have only lost three times in their last 11 games. Their sin? All three of those losses happened after we went out on a limb to bump them up to No. 14.
Sixers are 8-4 in March, including wins over Jazz and Heat, after beating Phoenix on the last day of February. But even in the East, they appear out of playoff range.
Stubborn Sixers were never going to rally all the way into the playoffs, but they do still have a better record since the Iverson trade than Denver at 24-26 to Nuggets' 22-27.
Cheeks speak: ''I heard people saying we might be winning too many games.'' Our reaction after Sixers move to 14-9 since the break: Who ever used the word ''might?''
Friends in Philly tell me you can't try to improve your pick and keep fans on your side. Tell us, locals: Do you prefer the league's 10th-best record (17-10) since the break?

ind.summary: The impact newcomer in Indy is . . . Darrell Armstrong? Our man DA just posted back-to-back, double-digit scoring games after registering two all season in '05-06.
Something to talk about besides that mohawk: Harrington has averaged 24 ppg the past five games after totaling just 12 points in his first two games back in Indy.
Maybe a long trip can help Pacers find some harmony and/or tranquility. They can only hope so, with seven of the next nine on the road and five of those out West.
Pacers continue to look like a roller-coaster team even without Artest, but it's tough to punish them too severely here when 11 teams in the East are making out worse.
Disappointing as it was to lose a roadie at the buzzer to struggling Seattle, Pacers still have East's No. 4 record . . . when they've played only six home games.
After the last few years, Pacers are used to big letdowns by now. But the Jackson-Carlisle blowup strangely followed Jack's first two 20-point games this season.
If Pacers, in their ongoing quest to play a little faster, can generate 95 points or more, they're 10-2. Problem is, Indy is 3-11 when it falls short of that cutoff.
Distressing as it was to score 71 points in Saturday's Conseco loss to Wolves, Pacers are still No. 2 in the East in plus/minus: 7 road wins and 4 home defeats = +3.
Losing at home to Bobcats, right after winning in Detroit, was doubly discouraging for Indy, keeping it from going four games over .500 for the first time all season.
The easiest way to diffuse Jermaine's frustration? If Pacers can just get to a mere 93 points, they're 17-4. When they don't, unfortunately, Pacers are 1-12.
The good news: Pacers are unbeaten in '07 except when they play Dallas. The bad news: Pacers had chances to beat mighty Mavs twice and imploded both times.
Pacers have a cushy stretch to work in the new guys: 11 of the next 13 games are at home. On the flip side: Indy has slipped to .500 for the first time in a month.
Pacers might be an afterthought around town because of a little game Colts have next week, but they looked pretty good at home in sweeping Bulls, Heat and Raps.
Warriors were widely proclaimed winners in the big trade last month with Indy, but it's Pacers who have won six of seven to go a season-high five games over .500.
Artest is long gone. Stephen Jackson? Gone, too. Yet Indy still can't avoid trouble or its trademark inconsistency, dropping three straight at home after a 6-1 run.
Not the sort of consistency they hoped for: Pacers were two games over .500 when the big trade was made (20-18) and they're two games over .500 since (8-6).
A heavy home loss to Artest-less Kings is bad. But this is worse: Indy also lost at home this month to three other sub-.500 West teams: Warriors, Sonics and Nuggets.
Calling these guys Indy .500 is one of our pet lines, but I certainly didn't expect to be dusting it off anytime soon. Not with Pacers sitting at 29-24 as recently as Feb. 22.
Things have unraveled so thoroughly -- and so quickly in these nine straight defeats -- that my incessant Indy .500 jokes must feel far out of reach for Pacers.
It's a good thing Indy Sub-.500 finally beat Hawks on Saturday. Check out Pacers' next five games: Rockets and Spurs away, followed by Heat-Bulls-Cavs at home.
Only one team in a decade besides these Pacers slid from five games over .500 into a double-digit losing skid. Toronto was 29-21 in '01-02, then lost 13 straight.
Pacers obviously can't post the 9-0 finish needed to avoid Carlisle's first-ever losing season. But if they can beat SA sans O'Neal, maybe the playoffs aren't out of reach.
Indy can no longer finish .500, true, but with their first back-to-back wins since mid-February and still holding the tiebreaker over Orlando, Pacers aren't dead yet.
On Super Bowl Sunday, Pacers were 26-21 and riding a 6-1 surge. Since Peyton prevailed, Pacers are 9-24 and now out of the playoffs for the first time since 1997.

min.summary: Told you Wolves had a great rookie. What we didn't tell you is that his name, in Week 1, would be second-rounder Craig Smith (who?) and not Randy Foye.
Of all the coaches feeling pressure already -- Rivers, Stotts and, of course, Isiah -- Casey's seat could well be the toastiest with Wolves quickly slipping under .500.
Latest in a long line of road woes: Cavs start Snow and Wesley together in a not-so-spry backcourt, with Hughes out injured … and still pound Wolves by 16.
Wolves have mustered some grit, answering a 1-5 skid with a three-game win streak, but this ain't the Mike James we know and love: 0 points in the last 2 games?
Not a good week overall, but an encouraging ending with Wolves' road win in Philly and my man Mike James, after a rough Nov., starting the new month strong.
The mere possibility of hooking up with AI appears to have sparked KG, judging by the two huge games he strung together (win vs. Jazz, win at Bulls) after the news broke.
Interesting little factoid: Wolves losing their only two games all week, both on the road, leaves the mighty West with only seven teams above .500. We're just saying.
Some trivia to take KG's mind off missing out on A.I.: Did you know Wolves are one of only four teams (with Grizz, Hornets, Bobcats) never to play on Christmas Day?
If he's not going to be dealt away for Iverson, might as well give him the rock: Foye enters 2007 coming off his best five-game stretch so far, averaging 14.6 ppg.
Foye is finally getting regular burn and Blount is hotter than ever. All of which means KG is getting some help, which might explain why Wolves have won seven of nine.
New year, new lease on life for KG? With Blount and Foye surging, too, Wolves are 6-1 in 2007 and would have been 7-0 if not for that one-point home L to Clips.
After last Monday's win in Detroit, Wolves were a season-high four games over .500. Three losses and two suspensions (KG and Ricky Davis) later, Wolves are regrouping.
I'll say this about Wolves: With KG out there, they almost always play hard. Which might be enough to hold off up-and-down Clips and young, ailing Warriors for No. 8.
Not sure who might be the new scapegoat in Minny: Wolves are 2-5 since Casey's firing and a deflating 0-3 since so impressively halting Suns' 17-game win streak.
Just what Wolves needed: Hornets and Kings have rejoined a race that now has seven teams -- Nuggets, Clips, Warriors and even Blazers, too -- after two playoff spots.
KG just made his 10th All-Star appearance. Unless Wolves win the West, that'll be the most in league history without a Finals appearance, topping George Gervin's nine.
Dwane Casey is smiling somewhere. Even with Sunday's victory over Wiz, Wolves are 6-10 since Casey's dismissal and KG just dropped his first hint about leaving.
Wolves were 20-20 and 4-1 in OT games when Casey was fired. Since his departure? Wolves are 6-13 overall, 0-3 in OT and 1-3 in games decided by two points or less.
The good news? Wolves finally won a game in OT for Wittman last week by outlasting Lakers. The bad news? Wittman's Wolves are 2-8 since the All-Star break.
It's a good thing Wittman has KG's support because the numbers -- 10 consecutive road defeats and 10 losses in 13 games overall -- don't make for pleasant reading.
Before KG's buzzer-beater Sunday to beat Portland, Wolves' playoff push featured a 3-8 record in March, 12 losses in 16 games and one win in 13 road games.
Playoff push? Since the All-Star break, only three teams have worse records than Wolves' 6-15 mark. They are: Indy at 4-17, Memphis at 5-16 and Atlanta at 6-16.
The worst part? Now every win is a killer for KG's Wolves. Nine teams have worse records than they do and Wolves only keep their lottery pick if it's in the top 10.
Industry insiders say the Gatorade commercial will almost certainly stay in circulation during the playoffs. Everything else KG-related? Two losses shy of 50, stay tuned.

den.summary: 'Melo apologized for his opening night ejection and took the blame for both losses. I wouldn't worry about him, in other words. I'd be worried about Utah.
Nugs are in a quick hole to Utah already after becoming just the second team in history to open with three straight L's by three or fewer points, then losing K-Mart.
Denver went 19-6 minus K-Mart in '05-06 but picked its spots on when to rest him. These Nuggets are 4-2 without him but have no such option and 70-plus games left.
It's a tough concession for K-Mart fans (like me), but Nuggets are 8-2 without him, riding the 'Melo/Camby/JR/Miller quartet and with Evans filling in nicely.
Nuggets can't get too broken up about a home loss to Grizz when 'Melo's an All-Star lock already, J.R. might be Steal of the Summer and they're even outscoring Phoenix.
Nuggets' next four are all away and all in the East. They don't mind, either, because they've been much better on the road, as Pepsi losses to Hawks and Grizz suggest.
Nuggets have enough to fret about, obviously, but we regret to remind them that the sked only gets tougher. Denver has played a West-low eight games in its conference.
With Camby freshly injured and Melo and J.R. suspended, Iverson will hear Sixers West cracks about his new team. But it's still quite a trade coup for Denver.
This doesn't happen every day: Camby's return from injury to team up with Iverson means Nuggets now have the top two picks from the 1996 draft in their lineup.
With Melo's return still two weeks away, Iverson is only racking up losses (five in a row) and techs. He's up to seven Ts, just two behind Sheed's league-high nine.
How much is Melo missed? In this favorable stretch of schedule, Nuggets are just 4-8 with Iverson. They might pay for it at season's end, with 13 of final 18 on the road.
Bleak as it looked there for a while without Melo, Nuggets couldn't have set up his return much better after spanking Cavs and rallying past stunned Rockets in Houston.
Melo will have played only five games in his comeback by the time West coaches turn in their All-Star reserve picks Tuesday. Not much time to impress, in other words.
Tell me you're not surprised West coaches bypassed Melo after all that public ''support.'' Tell me you didn't think they'd admit it if they didn't plan to vote for him.
With Iverson ailing and the team dropping seven of eight before much-needed road wins at Indy and Milwaukee, Melo could barely celebrate his All-Star breakthrough.
Nuggets think they can win their first playoff series since 1994. But it's hard to really know what to expect until Melo and Iverson play more than six games together.
It's been a rough year all around for in-season trades. Defensively challenged Nuggets awoke Monday with a 2-7 record when Melo and Iverson are both healthy.
Word of advice, Nuggets. Savor the next seven games, five at home, because no one in the league faces a harder finish: 13 of the final 18 games on the road.
Such are the troubles for teams around them that a 2-2 week -- 2-1 in the games that featured Melo and Iverson together -- jumps struggling Nuggets nicely.
Almost everyone's struggling from No. 10 down. Before routing Lakers and Suns, Denver hadn't beaten a winning team since Jan. and was 0-9 vs. the West's top four.
Winning on LeBron's floor takes Iverson and Melo to 11-11 when both are in Nuggets' lineup, with Denver in the midst of a 6-2 uptick overall since its 1-3 start in March.
Team with the toughest closing schedule loses the easiest game left on that schedule at home to Sonics. Double uh-oh: Nuggets are 2-5 since that five-game win streak.
Talk about good timing. Before their crucial weekend wins over Mavs and Clips, Nuggets were -- no misprint -- a mere 1-24 when held below 100 points.
Facing Spurs in Round 1 can't feel like the biggest prize, but Nuggets uncorked their best ball all season -- starting 8-0 in April -- during their roughest schedule stretch.

gsw.summary: It's too early in the game to say Sports Guy was right and we were wrong about these guys. A deserved drop, but no panic buttons pressed here . . . yet.
Beating two of last season's 60-win teams (Dallas and Detroit) in the same week is nice, but Warriors can't stop there with nine of their next 10 games in Oakland.
They've been flying even with J-Rich at half-speed. But Nellie played only seven guys vs. Sonics, with Murphy, Diogu and now this better-than-ever Baron dinged up, too.
Baron's hurt worse than they thought. But this helps with the pain: Warriors stun Utah without him and Biedrins averages 13.5 ppg, 12.4 rpg, 2.88 bpg over eight games.
Wins over Jazz and Spurs were special, but Warriors just played 11 of 12 at home and went 7-5. So they're behind last season's 12-6 pace, with several roadies forthcoming.
Those two no-shows in Texas were hideous, but an 0-5 skid in games decided by five points or less hurts worse, including Sunday's fall-from-ahead loss in Seattle.
Warriors have yearned to see some East teams after facing only four in their first 24 games. But Sunday's loss at Toronto (sans Bosh) wasn't the most convincing start.
Wins in Boston and Orlando addressed Warriors' road woes, but their injury problem is only spreading, claiming Ellis, Murphy and Pietrus as its latest victims.
Warriors contribute to the MIP muddle as much as anyone with three big progress-makers of their own: Ellis, Biedrins and the out-of-nowhere Matt Barnes.
With the production he's getting from Barnes, Biedrins and now Azubuike, maybe Nellie should sit a few more regulars and ask Mully to sign more no-names.
Warriors haven't slipped more than two games below .500 all season. But that might be coming soon judging by their last three games . . . losses by 23, 15 and 20.
Now you know why Nellie went on that ''Where are our veterans?'' rant about Dunleavy and Murphy. It's because he wanted to find them and trade them.
With the second-fewest road victories in the league at 4-15, Golden State's playoff hopes might hinge on the six-game East trip that starts Tuesday in Cleveland.
Can't spell it out better than Baron Davis, who sounds as disgusted as we are when he says: ''How are we going to be a playoff team when we can't win on the road?''
Both starting guards are on the shelf and even Boston has two more road victories than Warriors do. My question, then: How are these guys still in the playoff hunt?
If Baron is back reasonably soon, Warriors are still right there, sitting just a game out of No. 8 in the West despite the fact we haven't seen them at full strength in ages.
As Warriors head East for five games, J-Rich says: 'This road trip will make or break the season.' If it's a bad trip? J-Rich adds: 'We might as well hang the playoffs up.'
The trip J-Rich called make or break is an 0-4 trip with one game left. No wonder Nellie waved the white flag, conceding that Warriors' playoff dream is now a fantasy.
More evidence that the West isn't as wild as advertised: Nellie publicly proclaimed Warriors were done -- and they should be with a 7-26 road record -- but they're not.
Did Nellie know what he was doing all along? By publicly waving the white flag about its playoff chances, maybe he took all the pressure off his suddenly hot young team.
Warriors are 8-2 with Baron back, but Clips are almost as hot. So this apparently won't be a replay of 10 years ago, when 36-46 was good enough for Clips to be No. 8.
The flipside to their road woes: Warriors have racked up more wins at home (27) than San Antonio (26) and all but three West teams: Mavs (33), Suns (31) and Jazz (29).
Lookie here: Warriors have won four of seven road games and played OK in the three losses (Lakers, Jazz, Spurs). They're now 11-4 with their first-choice team healthy.
If Warriors find a way to lock up the playoff spot they can now taste, word is they'll rename the arena again and officially change Nellie's nickname to ''The Oracle.''

orl.summary: First they pounded Chicago. Then Magic pulled a Chicago and lost their focus after hearing everyone gush about how good they looked in their first game.
D-Howard has had some quiet nights offensively, true, but he also just went for 21 points and 22 boards against Kevin Garnett. In other words, he's doing fine.
The new favorite to win the Southeast? The best regular-season team in Florida? As long as Shaq's out and Grant Hill is healthy, it's not as outrageous as it sounds.
Magic's only L in the past eight games came mere hours after last Monday's kudos here. We're guessing Orlando fans would thus prefer muted praise this week.
Best in the East? A tidy 6-2 against the West? On a 59-win pace? Twenty-nine wins in their last 40 games counting last season's 16-6 finish? It's early, yes, but it's all true.
Best in the East? OK, maybe not yet. But you can live with a home L to the vets from Detroit, even in a statement game, when D-Howard turns a mere 21 that same night.
Warned you about too much praise, Orlando. Since rising to No. 3, Magic are 3-5 and got punked in a rare TNT date by the draftee (May) passed in favor of Vazquez.
